enonce_markdown: Which of the following best defines the opportunity cost of a decision?

choix.texte: The money price paid for the good or service chosen
The total value of all the alternatives that were not chosen
The accounting cost of producing the good chosen
The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Because resources are scarce, every choice means giving something up. Opportunity cost is measured by what is sacrificed, not by the money spent.

### Solution

Opportunity cost is the value of the **next best alternative forgone** when a choice is made. A money price (option a) is only part of the story, the sum of all alternatives (option b) overstates it because only the single best alternative is lost, and a production cost (option c) is an accounting amount, not a sacrifice of alternatives.

**Answer: D.**

enonce_markdown:
Ngozi has a free afternoon of 4 hours. She can either give private lessons at 2 500 FCFA per hour or work at a market stall at 2 000 FCFA per hour. She cannot do both. She chooses to give private lessons.

Calculate the opportunity cost, in FCFA, of her decision, and explain why it is not 10 000 FCFA.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone, not the value of the option chosen.

### Solution

The alternative given up is the market stall: $4 \times 2\,000 = 8\,000$ FCFA.

The opportunity cost is therefore **8 000 FCFA**. The 10 000 FCFA ($4 \times 2\,500$) is the income from the option she chose; it is the benefit gained, not the benefit sacrificed.

enonce_markdown:
The table shows the production possibilities of an economy that produces only maize and cassava (thousand tonnes), with all resources fully employed.

| Point | Maize | Cassava |
|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 120 |
| B | 20 | 100 |
| C | 40 | 70 |
| D | 60 | 30 |
| E | 80 | 0 |

What is the opportunity cost, in tonnes of cassava, of producing one extra tonne of maize when the economy moves from C to D?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The opportunity cost of moving along a production possibility curve is the quantity of one good given up divided by the quantity of the other good gained.

### Solution

From C to D, maize rises from 40 to 60 (gain of 20) and cassava falls from 70 to 30 (loss of 40).

Opportunity cost per tonne of maize $= 40 \div 20 = 2$ tonnes of cassava.

Option b (1.5) is the cost for the move from B to C ($30 \div 20$); option a (0.5) inverts the ratio; option d (40) forgets to divide by the gain in maize.

**Answer: C.**

enonce_markdown:
A university has already paid 80 million FCFA, non-refundable, for architects' plans for a new laboratory. It now has funds of 200 million FCFA, enough either to complete the laboratory or to build a library costing 180 million FCFA.

When the university decides whether to complete the laboratory, which of the following is the opportunity cost of that decision?

choix.texte: The benefits that the library would have provided
The 80 million FCFA already paid for the plans
The 200 million FCFA needed to complete the laboratory
The 380 million FCFA spent on the plans and the laboratory

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Opportunity cost looks forward: it is the benefit of the best alternative that is lost by the decision still to be taken. Money already spent and not recoverable (a sunk cost) is not an opportunity cost.

### Solution

If the university completes the laboratory it can no longer build the library, so the benefits of the library are what is forgone.

The 80 million FCFA already paid cannot be recovered whatever the university decides, so it is a sunk cost (option b). The 200 million FCFA (option c) is the money cost of the laboratory, and 380 million FCFA (option d) just adds irrelevant figures.

**Answer: A.**

enonce_markdown:
Ebot earns 250 000 FCFA per month in a job. He is considering leaving it to follow a full-time course lasting 24 months. The tuition fees are 400 000 FCFA per year. His living costs would be the same whether he works or studies.

Calculate the opportunity cost, in FCFA, of following the course, showing your working, and state why living costs are left out.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The opportunity cost of a choice includes the money outlay specific to that choice plus the income given up. Costs that are the same under both options do not change with the decision and are excluded.

### Solution

- Tuition fees: $2 \times 400\,000 = 800\,000$ FCFA.
- Wages forgone: $24 \times 250\,000 = 6\,000\,000$ FCFA.

Opportunity cost $= 800\,000 + 6\,000\,000 =$ **6 800 000 FCFA**.

Living costs are incurred whichever option he takes, so nothing is given up because of the decision.

enonce_markdown:
A country's production possibility curve for cocoa and coffee is a straight line joining 600 thousand tonnes of cocoa (with no coffee) to 300 thousand tonnes of coffee (with no cocoa). Resources are fully employed.

Which of the following is the correct conclusion about opportunity cost along this curve?

choix.texte: The opportunity cost of cocoa rises as more cocoa is produced
Each extra tonne of cocoa costs a constant 0.5 tonne of coffee
Each extra tonne of cocoa costs a constant 2 tonnes of coffee
The opportunity cost of cocoa falls as more cocoa is produced

corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The slope of a production possibility curve measures the opportunity cost. A straight line has a constant slope, so the opportunity cost is constant; a curve bowed outwards from the origin means increasing opportunity cost.

### Solution

Moving from all coffee to all cocoa, 300 coffee is given up for 600 cocoa, so each tonne of cocoa costs $300 \div 600 = 0.5$ tonne of coffee, at every point of the line. This happens when the factors of production are equally suited to both goods.

Option c (2) inverts the ratio and gives the opportunity cost of coffee in terms of cocoa; options a and d wrongly describe a bowed curve.

**Answer: B.**
